sections.name: Cinematic Rendering & Lighting
sections.explanation_simple: Rendering is turning your 3D scene into a final image or animation. The render engine calculates how light bounces around the scene - from light sources, off surfaces, into the camera. Cinematic rendering (for films) can take minutes to hours per frame but looks photorealistic. Real-time rendering (for games) runs at 60 frames per second but uses tricks to look good fast. The same principles of lighting apply to both: 3-point lighting (key, fill, rim), color temperature (warm/cool), and exposure control are universal whether you're rendering for a movie or a game.
key_concepts: Path Tracing: Tracing light rays from camera, bouncing off surfaces until they hit a light source
Bounces: How many times a light ray can bounce (more = realistic but slower)
Direct Lighting: Light directly from a source to a surface
Indirect Lighting: Light that bounces off one surface to another (the bounce light under a chin)
Global Illumination: All light interactions in a scene (direct + indirect)
HDRI: High Dynamic Range Image used for environment lighting (real-world light captured as image)
3-Point Lighting: Key light (main), Fill light (softens shadows), Rim light (separates from background)
Color Temperature: Measured in Kelvin (warm 3200K = indoor, cool 5600K = daylight)
Exposure: How much light enters the virtual camera (controls brightness)
Depth of Field: Blurring objects outside the focal plane (f-stop controls amount)
Motion Blur: Blurring fast-moving objects (shutter speed controls amount)
Bloom: Light bleeding from bright areas (glow effect)
Lens Flares: Artifacts from bright lights hitting the lens
Vignette: Darkening of image corners
Render Passes: Separate layers (diffuse, specular, shadows, AO, normal) for compositing flexibility
ACES: Industry standard color pipeline (Academy Color Encoding System)

code_examples.title: Blender Cycles: Cinematic Render Settings
code_examples.code:
# ===== BLENDER CYCLES CINEMATIC RENDER SETUP =====
import bpy

def setup_cinematic_render(scene_name="Scene", output_path="//renders/"):
    """Configure Blender Cycles for cinematic quality output."""

    scene = bpy.data.scenes.get(scene_name)
    if not scene:
        scene = bpy.context.scene

    # Set render engine to Cycles
    scene.render.engine = 'CYCLES'

    # Resolution: Cinema 4K (4096x2160)
    scene.render.resolution_x = 4096
    scene.render.resolution_y = 2160
    scene.render.resolution_percentage = 100
    scene.render.fps = 24  # Film standard

    # Cycles settings
    cycles = scene.cycles
    cycles.samples = 1024  # High quality (lower = faster, grainier)
    cycles.use_adaptive_sampling = True  # Adaptive: more samples in complex areas
    cycles.adaptive_threshold = 0.01  # Quality threshold
    cycles.adaptive_min_samples = 128  # Minimum before adaptive kicks in
    cycles.max_bounces = 8  # Total light bounces
    cycles.diffuse_bounces = 4
    cycles.glossy_bounces = 4
    cycles.transmission_bounces = 8  # Glass/transparent
    cycles.volume_bounces = 2
    cycles.transparent_max_bounces = 8

    # Denoising
    cycles.use_denoising = True
    cycles.denoiser = 'OPENIMAGEDENOISE'
    cycles.denoising_input_passes = 'RGB_ALBEDO_NORMAL'  # Best quality
    cycles.denoising_prefilter = 'ACCURATE'

    # Motion blur
    scene.render.use_motion_blur = True
    scene.render.motion_blur_shutter = 0.5  # 180-degree shutter rule
    scene.render.motion_blur_samples = 16

    # Color management (ACES)
    scene.view_settings.view_transform = 'AgX'  # AgX is the new ACES-like transform
    scene.view_settings.look = 'None'
    scene.view_settings.exposure = 0.0
    scene.view_settings.gamma = 1.0

    # Output settings
    scene.render.image_settings.file_format = 'OPEN_EXR_MULTILAYER'
    scene.render.image_settings.color_mode = 'RGBA'
    scene.render.image_settings.color_depth = '32'
    scene.render.image_settings.exr_codec = 'ZIP'

    # File path
    scene.render.filepath = output_path + scene_name + "_####"  # Frame number padding

    print(f"Cinematic render configured: {scene.render.resolution_x}x{scene.render.resolution_y} @ {scene.render.fps}fps")
    print(f"Samples: {cycles.samples}, Max bounces: {cycles.max_bounces}")

# setup_cinematic_render("MyScene", "//output/cinematic/")

# ===== BLENDER: 3-POINT LIGHTING SETUP =====
def setup_three_point_lighting(target_object_name="Subject"):
    """Create a classic 3-point lighting setup."""

    target = bpy.data.objects.get(target_object_name)
    if not target:
        print(f"Object '{target_object_name}' not found")
        return

    # Remove existing lights
    for obj in bpy.data.objects:
        if obj.type == 'LIGHT':
            bpy.data.objects.remove(obj, do_unlink=True)

    # 1. KEY LIGHT (Main light - 45 degrees to the side, 45 degrees up)
    bpy.ops.object.light_add(type='AREA', location=(2, -2, 3))
    key = bpy.context.active_object
    key.name = "Key_Light"
    key.data.energy = 800
    key.data.color = (1.0, 0.95, 0.9)  # Slightly warm
    key.data.size = 1.0  # Soft shadows
    # Aim at target
    constraint = key.constraints.new(type='TRACK_TO')
    constraint.target = target
    constraint.track_axis = 'TRACK_NEGATIVE_Z'
    constraint.up_axis = 'UP_Y'

    # 2. FILL LIGHT (Opposite side, softer - 45 degrees, slightly lower)
    bpy.ops.object.light_add(type='AREA', location=(-2, 1.5, 2))
    fill = bpy.context.active_object
    fill.name = "Fill_Light"
    fill.data.energy = 300  # Weaker than key (1:2 or 1:3 ratio)
    fill.data.color = (0.9, 0.92, 1.0)  # Slightly cool
    fill.data.size = 2.0  # Softer shadows
    constraint = fill.constraints.new(type='TRACK_TO')
    constraint.target = target
    constraint.track_axis = 'TRACK_NEGATIVE_Z'
    constraint.up_axis = 'UP_Y'

    # 3. RIM/BACK LIGHT (Behind subject, separates from background)
    bpy.ops.object.light_add(type='AREA', location=(0, 3, 2.5))
    rim = bpy.context.active_object
    rim.name = "Rim_Light"
    rim.data.energy = 400
    rim.data.color = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0)  # Neutral white
    rim.data.size = 0.5  # Harder edge for rim
    constraint = rim.constraints.new(type='TRACK_TO')
    constraint.target = target
    constraint.track_axis = 'TRACK_NEGATIVE_Z'
    constraint.up_axis = 'UP_Y'

    print("3-point lighting created: Key (800W), Fill (300W), Rim (400W)")

sections.name: Video Production, Compositing & CGI
sections.explanation_simple: CGI (Computer Generated Imagery) is combining computer-generated 3D elements with live-action footage. This is how movies create monsters, environments, and effects that don't exist in real life. Compositing is the art of combining these elements into a seamless final image. You shoot actors on a green screen, render your 3D elements, and then composite them together - matching colors, lighting, and camera movement so the viewer can't tell what's real and what's CGI. Nuke is the industry standard compositing tool (used by every major VFX studio), but DaVinci Resolve is a powerful free alternative.
key_concepts: Green Screen/Chroma Key: Shooting actors against a green background that gets removed digitally
Keying: Removing the green/blue screen to isolate the subject
Spill: Green light reflecting onto the subject (green glow on edges)
Match Moving: Tracking camera movement in live footage so 3D elements match
Camera Tracking: Solving for camera position and movement from 2D footage
Planar Tracking: Tracking flat surfaces (screens, signs, walls) for adding graphics
Rotoscoping: Manually tracing objects frame by frame (painful but sometimes necessary)
Render Passes: Rendering 3D elements as separate layers (diffuse, shadows, reflections) for compositing
CG Integration: Making CG look like it belongs in the live-action footage
Color Grading: Adjusting colors to create a consistent look across all shots
LUT: Look-Up Table - a preset color transformation (used for consistent color grading)
Virtual Cinematography: Placing and animating cameras in 3D to create film-like shots
Motion Graphics: Animated graphic design elements (titles, lower thirds, data visualization)

code_examples.title: DaVinci Resolve: Fusion Compositing Workflow
code_examples.code:
# ===== FUSION COMPOSITING WORKFLOW IN DAVINCI RESOLVE =====
"""
NODE TREE FOR CGI INTEGRATION:

INPUTS:
  MediaIn1 (Live action plate - actor on green screen)
  MediaIn2 (CG render - 3D monster with alpha)

COMPOSITING FLOW:

  MediaIn1                     MediaIn2
     |                            |
  DeltaKeyer (remove green)    AlphaMultiply (apply alpha)
     |                            |
  ColorCorrector (fix spill)   ColorCorrector (match lighting)
     |                            |
  EdgeExtend (fix edges)       Blur (match camera focus)
     |                            |
     +--------- Merge -----------+
                    |
               ColorCorrector (grade entire shot)
                    |
              Glow/ lens flare
                    |
               MediaOut

KEY NODES:
  - DeltaKeyer: Best keyer in Fusion, handles fine details (hair, smoke)
  - ColorCorrector: Primary color correction (lift, gamma, gain)
  - Merge: Combines two inputs with blending modes
  - Blur: Match depth of field between CG and plate
  - Tracker: Match move the CG element to the plate
  - PlanarTracker: Track flat surfaces for screen replacements
"""

// Fusion script to set up a basic composite
// This can be run in Fusion's Console

comp = fusion.CurrentComp

-- Create nodes
mediaIn1 = comp:AddTool("MediaIn", -32768, -32768)
mediaIn1.Name = "Live_Action_Plate"

keyer = comp:AddTool("DeltaKeyer", -32768, -16384)
keyer.Name = "Green_Screen_Key"
keyer.Inputs.BackgroundColor = { 0, 1, 0 } -- Green
keyer.Inputs.Tolerance = 0.15
keyer.Inputs.Soften = 0.5

mediaIn2 = comp:AddTool("MediaIn", -16384, -32768)
mediaIn2.Name = "CG_Render"

merge = comp:AddTool("Merge", 0, -16384)
merge.Name = "Composite"

colorCorrect = comp:AddTool("ColorCorrector", 16384, -16384)
colorCorrect.Name = "Final_Grade"

mediaOut = comp:AddTool("MediaOut", 32768, -16384)
mediaOut.Name = "Output"

-- Connect nodes
comp:Connect(mediaIn1.Output, keyer.Inputs.Input)
comp:Connect(mediaIn2.Output, merge.Inputs.Foreground)
comp:Connect(keyer.Output, merge.Inputs.Background)
comp:Connect(merge.Output, colorCorrect.Inputs.Input)
comp:Connect(colorCorrect.Output, mediaOut.Inputs.Input)

print("Basic composite setup created")

-- ===== BLENDER: CAMERA TRACKING =====
"""
1. Import your video footage as a movie clip
2. Switch to Movie Clip Editor
3. Set tracking settings (default is usually fine)
4. Add track points on high-contrast features in the footage
5. Track forward and backward through the clip
6. Solve camera motion (set focal length correctly!)
7. Set up ground plane and 3D scene scale
8. Add your 3D objects - they now move with the footage
9. Render and composite
"""

sections.name: AI-Powered 3D Creation & Neural Rendering
sections.explanation_simple: AI is revolutionizing 3D creation. You can now generate 3D models from text descriptions (text-to-3D), create realistic textures from a single image, animate characters with AI motion synthesis, upscale low-res textures to 4K, and even generate entire 3D scenes. Tools like Runway, Cascadeur, DeepMotion, and Wonder Dynamics use AI to automate the hardest parts of 3D creation - especially animation. AI isn't replacing artists yet, but it's making them 10x faster by handling the tedious parts. Think of AI as a super-powered assistant who does the boring work so you can focus on the creative decisions.
key_concepts: AI Animation Generation: Tools that create character animation from video (DeepMotion, Cascadeur)
AI Physics: Automatically adding realistic physics to animations (Cascadeur's auto-physics)
AI Motion Synthesis: Generating new animations from existing motion data
AI Texture Generation: Creating textures from text prompts (Stable Diffusion for textures)
AI Upscaling: Increasing texture resolution 4x-16x while preserving detail (ESRGAN, Topaz Gigapixel)
AI Lip Sync: Automatically syncing mouth movements to audio (NVIDIA Audio2Face)
AI Rigging: Automatically creating skeletons from 3D meshes (AccuRig, Auto-Rig Pro)
AI Scene Generation: Creating 3D scenes from text descriptions (Luma AI, NeRFs)
Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF): Creating 3D scenes from 2D photos (AI-based photogrammetry)
Diffusion Models: AI that generates images from noise (Stable Diffusion, Midjourney for concept art)
Neural Rendering: Using AI to enhance rendered images (DLSS, denoising, super-resolution)
Denoising: AI removes noise from renders, allowing fewer samples (faster render times)
NVIDIA DLSS: Deep Learning Super Sampling - AI upscaling for games (renders at lower res, outputs higher)

# ===== AI TEXTURE GENERATION WORKFLOW =====
"""
Using AI to generate PBR textures from text prompts:

1. GENERATE BASE TEXTURE
   Tool: Stable Diffusion + ControlNet
   Prompt: "red brick wall, weathered, mortar, photorealistic, 4k"
   Control: Canny edge of your UV layout or a rough sketch
   Output: 2048x2048 image

2. GENERATE PBR MAPS
   Tool: Stable Diffusion with PBR adapter or Materialize (free tool)
   Input: The generated base color image
   Output: Normal map, Roughness map, Displacement map

3. TILE THE TEXTURE
   Tool: Any texture tiling tool (PixPlant, Substance Sampler)
   Make sure edges match seamlessly

4. APPLY IN BLENDER/UNREAL
   Import as PBR material
   Adjust tiling, roughness multiplier, etc.
"""

# Python: Using Stable Diffusion API for texture generation
import requests
import json
import base64
from PIL import Image
import io

def generate_pbr_texture(prompt, output_path="texture.png", width=1024, height=1024):
    """
    Generate a PBR texture using Stable Diffusion API.
    Requires a running Stable Diffusion WebUI with API enabled.
    """
    url = "http://localhost:7860/sdapi/v1/txt2img"

    payload = {
        "prompt": prompt + ", photorealistic, highly detailed, pbr texture, tileable",
        "negative_prompt": "cartoon, low quality, blurry, distorted",
        "steps": 30,
        "width": width,
        "height": height,
        "cfg_scale": 7.5,
        "sampler_name": "Euler a",
        "seed": -1,
        "tiling": True,  # Make texture tileable
    }

    response = requests.post(url, json=payload)

    if response.status_code == 200:
        # Decode base64 image
        img_data = response.json()['images'][0]
        img_bytes = base64.b64decode(img_data)
        img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(img_bytes))
        img.save(output_path)
        print(f"Texture saved to {output_path}")
        return True
    else:
        print(f"Error: {response.status_code}")
        return False

# Usage:
# generate_pbr_texture("weathered medieval stone wall, moss, detailed mortar lines")

# ===== AI MOTION CAPTURE WITH DEEPMOTION =====
"""
DeepMotion (deepmotion.com) - AI motion capture from video

WORKFLOW:
1. Record a video of a person moving
2. Upload to DeepMotion
3. AI extracts 3D skeleton and motion
4. Download as FBX with animation
5. Import into Blender/Unreal
6. Retarget to your character

OR use Animate3D API:
"""

import requests

def animate_with_ai(video_path, output_path="animation.fbx"):
    """Send video to AI mocap service and download result."""

    api_key = "YOUR_DEEPMOTION_API_KEY"
    url = "https://api.deepmotion.com/v1/animation"

    # Upload video
    with open(video_path, 'rb') as f:
        files = {'video': f}
        headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}'}
        response = requests.post(url, files=files, headers=headers)

    if response.status_code == 200:
        job_id = response.json()['job_id']
        print(f"Animation job started: {job_id}")

        # Poll for completion
        import time
        while True:
            status = requests.get(f"{url}/{job_id}", headers=headers)
            data = status.json()
            if data['status'] == 'completed':
                # Download result
                download_url = data['download_url']
                result = requests.get(download_url)
                with open(output_path, 'wb') as out:
                    out.write(result.content)
                print(f"Animation saved to {output_path}")
                break
            elif data['status'] == 'failed':
                print(f"Animation failed: {data.get('error', 'Unknown error')}")
                break
            time.sleep(5)
    else:
        print(f"Upload failed: {response.status_code}")

Cascadeur - AI-assisted character animation
- Auto-physics: Automatically adds realistic physics to keyframes

sections.name: Industry Asset Pipelines, USD & Production Standards
sections.explanation_simple: Asset pipelines are the systems and processes that move 3D assets from creation tools to the final game or film. A AAA game asset goes through: concept art -> 3D modeling -> sculpting -> retopology -> UV mapping -> baking -> texturing -> rigging -> animation -> LOD creation -> engine import -> materials setup -> testing. Each step has specific standards (polygon counts, texture sizes, naming conventions). USD (Universal Scene Description) from Pixar is the industry standard for exchanging data between different 3D applications. It's like a universal language that Maya, Houdini, Katana, and Unreal Engine all understand.
key_concepts: USD (Universal Scene Description): Pixar's open-source framework for 3D scene interchange
USD Layers: Non-destructive overrides (base model + variant layers for different LODs)
USD Composition: Combining assets from different sources into one scene
Alembic (.abc): Open format for animated geometry and particle caches
FBX: Common format for transferring assets between applications (limited compared to USD)
glTF: 'JPEG of 3D' - standard for real-time 3D on web and mobile
Asset Naming Conventions: Standardized names (weapon_sword_iron_v01, human_male_base_mesh)
Asset Validation: Automated checks (poly count, scale, naming, missing textures)
LOD Pipeline: Automatic generation of LODs from high-poly source
Texture Budget: Total texture memory per asset (e.g., 2x 2K textures per character)
Texel Density: Consistent pixels-per-unit across all assets in a project
Scene Optimization: Removing unseen faces, merging materials, reducing draw calls
Version Control for Assets: Perforce, Git LFS, or Subversion for binary files
Shotgun/FTrack: Production tracking software for managing asset pipelines
Render Farm: Network of computers that process render frames in parallel

# ===== BLENDER: AUTO-EXPORT TO GAME ENGINE =====
import bpy
import os

def export_game_asset(mesh_name, output_dir, export_format='FBX'):
    """Export a Blender mesh to game engine format with LODs."""

    obj = bpy.data.objects.get(mesh_name)
    if not obj:
        print(f"Object '{mesh_name}' not found")
        return

    # Select and make active
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = obj
    obj.select_set(True)

    # Ensure scale is applied
    bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(location=False, rotation=False, scale=True)

    # Generate LODs
    lods = [100, 50, 25, 10]  # Percent of original faces
    for i, percentage in enumerate(lods):
        # Create LOD by decimation
        modifier = obj.modifiers.new(name=f"LOD_{i}_Decimate", type='DECIMATE')
        modifier.ratio = percentage / 100.0

        # Export each LOD
        if export_format == 'FBX':
            output_path = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{obj.name}_LOD{i}.fbx")
            bpy.ops.export_scene.fbx(
                filepath=output_path,
                use_selection=True,
                apply_scale_option='FBX_SCALE_UNITS',
                mesh_smooth_type='FACE',
                use_mesh_modifiers=True,
                bake_anim=False
            )
            print(f"Exported: {output_path}")

        # Remove the modifier before next LOD
        obj.modifiers.remove(modifier)

    print(f"All LODs exported for {mesh_name}")


# ===== ASSET VALIDATION SCRIPT =====
def validate_game_asset(obj):
    """Check if an asset meets game-ready standards."""
    issues = []

    # Check polygon count
    face_count = len(obj.data.polygons)
    if face_count > 50000:
        issues.append(f"High poly count: {face_count} (max 50K for hero asset)")
    elif face_count > 100000:
        issues.append(f"Extreme poly count: {face_count} (max 100K for cinematic)")

    # Check UVs exist
    if not obj.data.uv_layers:
        issues.append("No UV layers!")

    # Check UV overlap
    # (basic check - full overlap check is more complex)
    uv_layer = obj.data.uv_layers.active.data
    uv_set = set()
    for uv in uv_layer:
        coord = (round(uv.uv.x, 4), round(uv.uv.y, 4))
        uv_set.add(coord)
    if len(uv_set) < len(uv_layer) * 0.5:
        issues.append("UVs may be overlapping (many duplicate coordinates)")

    # Check scale
    if abs(obj.scale.x - 1.0) > 0.01 or abs(obj.scale.y - 1.0) > 0.01 or abs(obj.scale.z - 1.0) > 0.01:
        issues.append(f"Scale not applied: ({obj.scale.x:.2f}, {obj.scale.y:.2f}, {obj.scale.z:.2f})")

    # Check materials
    if not obj.material_slots:
        issues.append("No materials assigned")

    # Check for ngons (faces with >4 vertices)
    ngons = [p for p in obj.data.polygons if len(p.vertices) > 4]
    if ngons:
        issues.append(f"{len(ngons)} ngon faces found (should be tris or quads)")

    # Check vertex normals
    obj.data.calc_normals_split()
    # Basic check - if normals are there

    if issues:
        print(f"=== ASSET VALIDATION: {obj.name} ===")
        for issue in issues:
            print(f"  [!] {issue}")
    else:
        print(f"[OK] {obj.name} passes validation")

    return len(issues) == 0

# ===== USD EXPORT FROM BLENDER =====
import bpy

def export_to_usd(obj_name="Model", output_path="//exports/model.usdc"):
    """Export a Blender object as USD for Unreal Engine."""

    obj = bpy.data.objects.get(obj_name)
    if not obj:
        print(f"Object '{obj_name}' not found")
        return

    # Select the object
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = obj
    obj.select_set(True)

    # Set up USD export
    bpy.ops.wm.usd_export(
        filepath=output_path,
        selected_objects_only=True,
        export_materials=True,
        export_uvmaps=True,
        export_normals=True,
        export_animation=False,
        use_instancing=True,
        export_textures=True,  # Embeds textures or references them
        convert_orientation=True,  # Z-up to Y-up for Unreal
        scale=100.0  # cm to m (if needed)
    )

    print(f"Exported {obj_name} to USD: {output_path}")

# ===== USD LAYERS (Non-destructive overrides) =====
"""
USD's layer system is revolutionary for pipelines:

Main.usd (composite of all layers)
    |
    +-- Base.usda (base model - from modeling department)
    |       - Geometry, base UVs
    |
    +-- Material_overrides.usda (from lookdev department)
    |       - Overrides materials (without touching geometry)
    |       - Non-destructive! Can be updated independently
    |
    +-- Animation.usda (from animation department)
    |       - Overrides transform and bone animation
    |
    +-- Variant_LOD.usda (from tech art)
            - Variant set for LOD switching
            - Each variant selects different LOD mesh

Each department can update their layer WITHOUT affecting others.
This is the big advantage over FBX where everything is baked.
"""

# Python: Create a USD layer override
from pxr import Usd, UsdGeom, Sdf

def create_usd_variants(usd_path, variants):
    """Create variant sets for LOD switching."""

    stage = Usd.Stage.Open(usd_path)
    prim = stage.GetPrimAtPath("/Root")

    # Create variant set
    variant_set = prim.GetVariantSets().AddVariantSet("LOD")

    for name, filepath in variants.items():
        variant_set.AddVariant(name)
        variant_set.SetVariantSelection(name)

        with variant_set.GetVariantEditContext():
            # Reference the LOD mesh
            prim.GetReferences().AddReference(filepath)

    stage.GetRootLayer().Save()
    print(f"Created LOD variants: {list(variants.keys())}")

# Usage:
# create_usd_variants("char.usdc", {
#     "LOD0": "char_lod0.usdc",
#     "LOD1": "char_lod1.usdc",
#     "LOD2": "char_lod2.usdc"
# })
